L13: # High temperature (fever) in adults
L14: 
L15: A high temperature (fever) is usually a symptom of an infection. It often improves on its own and there are things you can do at home to help treat it.
L16: ## What is a high temperature?
L17: 
L18: Normal body temperature is different for everyone and changes during the day.
L19: 
L20: A high temperature is usually considered to be 38C or above. This is sometimes called a fever.
L21: ## Check if you have a high temperature
L22: 
L23: You may have a high temperature if:
L24: 
L25:   * your chest or back feels hotter than usual
L26:   * you have other symptoms, such as feeling hot or cold, feeling shivery (chills), sweating, or your skin being warm and red (this may be harder to see on black or brown skin)
L27:   * a thermometer says your temperature is 38C or above
L28: 
L29: ### Important
L30: 
L31: If you feel hot, cold or shivery, you may have a high temperature even if a thermometer says your temperature is below 38C.
L32: ### Taking your temperature
L33: 
L34: You do not need to take your temperature using a thermometer, but you can if you have one.
L35: 
L36: Make sure you use it correctly to help get an accurate result.
L37: 
L38: How to take your temperature with a digital thermometer
L39: 
L40: To use a digital thermometer:
L41:   1. Clean the tip with cold water and soap, then rinse it.
L42:   2. Turn the thermometer on.
L43:   3. Put the tip under your tongue, towards the back of your mouth.
L44:   4. Close your lips around the thermometer.
L45:   5. Wait until it beeps or flashes.
L46:   6. Remove the thermometer and check the temperature on the display.
L47: 
L48: You can also use a digital thermometer in your armpit. Make sure you keep your arm tight against your body until the thermometer beeps or flashes.
L49: Directions may vary depending on the thermometer. Always follow the instructions that come with it.
L50: ### Other types of thermometer
L51: 
L52: If you use a digital ear thermometer, follow the instructions that come with it. You usually need to gently pull your ear up and back before putting the thermometer in your ear.
L53: 
L54: Do not use:
L55: 
L56:   * a glass thermometer because they can be dangerous
L57:   * an infrared thermometer because some do not meet UK regulations
L58:   * forehead strips because they're not accurate
L59: 
L60: Information:
L61: ### Advice for children and babies
L62: 
L63: This page is for adults. For advice about children and babies, including how to take a temperature, see:
L64: 
L65:   * 【6†high temperature (fever) in children】
L66:   * 【7†how to take your baby's temperature】
L67: 
L68: ## Treating a high temperature
L69: 
L70: There are some things you can do to help treat a high temperature.
L71: ### Do
L72: 
L73:   * get lots of rest
L74: 
L75:   * drink plenty of fluids (water is best) to avoid dehydration – drink enough so your pee is light yellow and clear
L76: 
L77:   * take 【8†paracetamol】 or 【9†ibuprofen】 if you feel uncomfortable
L78: 
L79: Information:
L80: 
L81: Try to stay at home and avoid contact with other people until you do not have a high temperature.
L82: 
L83: ## When and where to get medical help
L84: 
L85: Most high temperatures get better on their own, but sometimes you may need medical help.
L86: ### Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if you have:
L87: 
L88:   * a high temperature and you've been treating it at home but it's not getting better or is getting worse
L89: 
L90: You can call 111 or 【10†get help from 111 online†111.nhs.uk】.
L91: ## Causes of a high temperature
L92: 
L93: Many things can cause a high temperature. It's not usually a sign of anything serious.
L94: 
L95: It's often just caused by your body fighting an infection, such as a 【11†cold】 or 【12†flu】.
L96: 
L97: Sometimes it could be a sign of something more serious if your temperature is very high or will not come down.
L98:
